title: Fly Higher with More Twist: The Optimization of a Half-Pipe

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF page 1 is the MCM summary sheet; the body page footer begins at Page 1 on PDF page 2.

context_sources.use: Authoritative statement for vertical air, twist, and practical-course tasks.

limitations: All 30 pages were rendered at 144 DPI and reviewed through six contact sheets.
Text extraction corrupts several Greek letters and degree symbols; formulas and symbols were checked against rendered pages.
The public appendix includes MATLAB fragments but not one end-to-end regeneration script.
No official judge commentary explains the Finalist decision.

required_outputs: Design half-pipe geometry to maximize vertical air.
Tailor the design to another performance requirement, here aerial twist.
Determine tradeoffs needed for a practical course.
paper_interpretation: Use work-energy and repeated-cycle geometry to size height, angle, width, radius, and length.
Use sport-biomechanics and a rotation proxy to select geometry for twist.
Use an external score equation to combine vertical air and twist.
Compare alternative cross-sections and propose drag and safety refinements.
task_reconstruction.coverage_note: All three questions receive numerical or qualitative answers, but the reported final design is not jointly reoptimized under one consistent geometry, utility, and practical constraint set.

section_map.summary: Answers Questions One through Three in task order and reports a complete design vector.
Provides detailed navigation through models, verification, sensitivity, strengths, refinements, references, and code.
Links performance metrics to half-pipe geometry and previews Dynamics and Sport Biomechanics.
Defines three half-pipe families and selects a circular-transition flat-bottom design.
States assumptions, cross-section geometry, force balance, friction, and athlete work.
Derives platform height, transition angle, radius, flat width, and total course length.
Introduces bending-twist compliance and a takeoff-to-aerial-rotation proxy.
Uses score-regression coefficients to aggregate vertical-air and twist optima.
Qualitatively compares elliptical transitions and an arced flat.
Compares dimensions with existing venues and sweeps initial speed.
Lists claimed simplicity, breadth, assumptions, and data limitations.
Adds a symbolic drag term and proposes a safety relation.
Publishes MATLAB fragments for angle optimization, geometry, and sensitivity plots.

contributions.summary: Maps each official question to a method and concrete answer, which makes a long multi-stage paper easy to triage.
Connects three performance metrics to a named geometry vector before presenting the models.
Makes the intended geometry, friction, athlete-work, and vertical-air dependencies explicit.
Reports height, radius, angle, flat width, and course length with values and units.
Attempts to translate a published acceleration trace into a required flat distance.
Recognizes that venue geometry alone is insufficient and tries to incorporate biomechanics and rotation.
Recognizes that vertical air and twist compete and relates them to a scoring equation.
Checks facility-scale plausibility and exposes how the design changes with entry speed.
Makes optimizer constants and sensitivity arrays inspectable through a MATLAB appendix.

dependency_graph.main_flow: entry speed -> platform height and acceleration law -> transition-angle response -> radius, width, and length -> twist proxy -> score tradeoff
dependency_graph.extensions: baseline geometry -> alternative shapes; energy and speed laws -> drag and safety refinements
broken_or_missing_links: The angle optimizer uses provisional radius and width rather than the final geometry.
The compliance relation does not feed the reported twist optimum.
The score model does not directly optimize predicted score over geometry.
Drag and safety are not propagated to a revised design.

assumptions.summary: Treats rider and snowboard as one entity and ignores aerodynamic drag in the baseline.
Assumes vertical air for a specific athlete is constant, which conflicts with the stated optimization target.
Approximates transition friction with a constant-normal-load path expression.
Treats one published accelerometer trace as a transferable one-second linear pumping law.
Assumes approximately seven identical flight cycles and same-height ballistic landings.
Assumes horizontal speed converts to aerial rotation with a constant efficiency.
Assumes regression coefficients with different units can be normalized into preference weights.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Imports an 11.06 m/s entry speed from a cited source without a distribution or transfer analysis.
Visually abstracts a published accelerometer plot into a two-segment law without digitized points or fit residuals.
Imports a predicted-score regression without its sample, uncertainty, units discussion, or valid domain.
Collects facility dimensions from several references for a scale-plausibility comparison.
Publishes hard-coded MATLAB inputs and sensitivity arrays but no raw measurement data.

models.summary: Geometry and work-energy model with 10 source-checked equations.
models.purpose: Relate geometry, friction, and athlete work to vertical air.

models.summary: Entry-speed energy conversion with 2 source-checked equations.
Bounded launch-angle optimization with 7 source-checked equations.
Repeated-cycle distance model with 8 source-checked equations.
Compliance and aerial-rotation proxy with 10 source-checked equations.
Qualitative comparison with an explicit omitted-by-paper equation status.
Incomplete refinement with 4 source-checked drag equations and an undefined safety bridge.

verification.summary: Shows a single-peaked internal response curve for the provisional angle-optimization inputs.
Compares reported dimensions with existing facility ranges; this supports scale plausibility, not mechanism validity.
Sweeps entry speed from 7 to 12 m/s but leaves other structural and parametric uncertainties fixed.
Exposes optimizer constants and sensitivity arrays but does not regenerate the full final design from one parameter set.

results_trace.summary: Question One: h_x=6.241 m follows from the cited 11.06 m/s entry speed under no loss.
Question One: delta=51.66 degrees is optimized on provisional geometry, then r_x=16.44 m is derived.
Question One: w_x=19.18 m follows from the one-second acceleration abstraction.
Question One: a_x=159.95 m follows from seven identical cycle advances.
Question Two: delta=45 degrees is claimed from a simplified sin(2 delta) proxy; no numerical twist angle is produced.
Question Three: delta_t=51.63 degrees is a weighted average of two separate optima, not a directly optimized combined objective.
Ellipse and arced-flat alternatives receive qualitative rather than matched quantitative comparisons.

writing_logic.summary: Strong task-indexed order keeps model names and design answers aligned with the three questions.
Detailed navigation reduces search cost across a long mechanics paper.
Moves from performance metrics to design variables and then to method families, but spends two opening sentences on generic background.
A parameter-by-parameter sequence makes the final design vector easy to follow.
The score relation provides a clear decision bridge, but the practical-course claim exceeds the represented constraints.
The paper distinguishes baseline omissions from later extensions, but the summary presents proposed refinements too strongly.
No conclusion section restates all three answers with evidence limits and unresolved practical conditions.

language_observations.summary: Seventeen sentence-level and two paragraph-level units capture task frames, model names, numerical design answers, comparison, verification, and refinement moves.
The strongest reusable pattern pairs each requested task with method, target quantity, value, unit, and conditions.
Interesting, best, ensures, tested, and refined require stronger objective, validation, and completion evidence than the body supplies.
Historical popularity and no-doubt technology claims are weak unless shortened and connected to a measurable design need.
The useful middle move narrows design diversity into explicit geometry variables and competing objectives.
The closing chain names metrics, geometry variables, method families, and objectives in the same order used by the body.
Trend language must agree with equations and tables; approximately linear needs a defined range and approximation error.

visualization_observations.summary: The labeled geometry diagram establishes height, radius, angle, flat width, and total width before equations.
A local launch diagram makes horizontal and vertical velocity components interpretable.
The response curve visually supports an interior scalar optimum but omits angular units, fixed inputs, and an optimum marker.
Showing both the source accelerometer trace and its simplified law is good transformation disclosure, though points and residuals are absent.
Sketches widen the design discussion but cannot rank shapes without matched geometry and response overlays.
A table plus trend plot supports conditional lookup, but uncertainty and recommendation reversal are absent.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The exact task-indexed design vector may improve first-page triage, but no judge evidence attributes Finalist status to it.
Navigation, notation, figures, and public MATLAB fragments may improve auditability, but causal judging relevance cannot be determined.

weaknesses.summary: The printed normal-force equation is dimensionally inconsistent with the following friction integrand.
Total and average active work differ by a factor of n.
The reported optimum is calculated on geometry different from the final reported design.
The flat-width result inherits an uncalibrated visual abstraction from one external trace.
The final twist equation drops 4/(l_0 g) and does not yield a dimensionally valid angle.
The model normalizes incompatible regression coefficients and averages separate argmax locations.
Range closeness and a one-factor sweep do not validate the performance mechanism or recommendation.
Drag contains a sign inconsistency and safety has no implemented outcome, threshold, or revised design.

independent_extensions.proposal: Replace the total-average work ambiguity with a phase-resolved athlete power or impulse model and calibrate it from rider data.
independent_extensions.reason: Active input is central to vertical air and cannot remain an unidentified sum.
independent_extensions.required_test: Energy closure and held-out trajectory comparison.

independent_extensions.proposal: Jointly optimize height, radius, angle, width, and length under one geometry and recompute every dependent state.
independent_extensions.reason: Sequentially replacing fixed inputs invalidates the reported optimum.

independent_extensions.proposal: Model aerial rotation from takeoff angular impulse, time-varying inertia, three-axis attitude, opening, and landing orientation.
independent_extensions.reason: Translational speed alone cannot determine twist.

independent_extensions.proposal: Optimize a unit-consistent utility or Pareto frontier over performance, safety, construction, footprint, and cost.
independent_extensions.reason: Regression coefficients with different units are not preference weights.
independent_extensions.required_test: Normalization audit, preference sensitivity, and Pareto dominance.

independent_extensions.proposal: Implement drag and safety within the state equations and rerun the full design rather than listing them as future terms.
independent_extensions.reason: A refinement is operational only when it changes predictions or decisions.
independent_extensions.required_test: Revised geometry, uncertainty, and recommendation reversal.

candidate_rule_impacts.rationale: Question-indexed architecture is strong, but practical and conclusion closure remain incomplete.
Tested, verified, refined, linear, and practical exceed the supplied evidence.
Task labels, contents, symbols, and numerical answers aid scanning, while generic background and symbol drift reduce clarity.
The design lacks matched geometry, contact, load, landing, safety, and construction closure.
Friction and drag are named separately but contain unit, sign, integration, and calibration defects.
Active work and acceleration are not phase-calibrated or athlete-validated and fail algebraic closure.
Rotation omits angular impulse, inertia, posture, three-axis motion, and landing and is dimensionally incomplete.
The reported optima use inconsistent geometry, incomplete objectives, and insufficient solver evidence.
Targets, inputs, equations, and physical objects are repeatedly circular, unused, or inconsistent.
Internal examples and facility-size plausibility are mislabeled as validation.
Only initial speed is swept and decision stability under coupled uncertainty is not tested.
Equation, code, table, figure, and prose do not form one regenerable specification.
Hard-coded sensitivity arrays and mismatched optimizer constants reveal missing equation-code parity and regression tests.
Response and alternative-design figures omit units, common constraints, feasibility events, and uncertainty.
A unit-consistent utility or Pareto formulation is required before combining performance objectives.

unresolved_questions: What measured athlete-work or pumping data support the vertical-air model?
Why did the angle optimizer use r_x=25 m and w_x=19.81 m instead of the final geometry?
What are the units and numerical values of chi, l_0, and the compliance coefficients?
What sample and validity range support the external score regression?
What source supports approximately seven identical flight cycles?
Were the drag and safety refinements ever propagated through the optimization outside the paper?
No judge commentary is available, so causal explanations for Finalist status remain conjectural.
